messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Conflict: Confrontations, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Vignette:
Mr. Binh presents as a quiet, seventy-six-year-old man whose physical stillness seems to conceal a deep and constant tension. He has worked the night shift at a large distribution warehouse for the last fifteen years, a job he chose for its solitude. For decades, the memories of his youth in a small village ravaged by war were something he could manage, distant and contained. But in recent years, they have begun to break through into his present with a new and terrifying intensity. The event itself remains etched in his mind with crystalline clarity. He was just a boy, not yet a man, when the soldiers came to his family’s home. He remembers the shouting first, the sharp, angry commands in a language he barely understood. Then, the splintering of the door. Before he could react, he was thrown to the floor, the side of his face pressed hard against the cool, damp earth. The smell of the soil filled his nostrils, mixed with the acrid scent of gunpowder and something else, something metallic. He felt a heavy boot on his back and the unyielding pressure of a hand gripping his neck, holding him down. He was utterly helpless, a witness to the chaos and violence that unfolded in the home around him.

This sensory imprint has followed him for over fifty years. Now, at the warehouse, something as simple as a colleague placing a firm, friendly hand on his shoulder to get his attention can send a jolt of pure panic through him. To Binh, it is not a touch; it is the beginning of being restrained, the weight of that boot on his back. The world around him dissolves in an instant, and without any warning, he is back on that dirt floor. The memory is not a thought but a full-body experience; he can feel the grit against his cheek and smell the damp earth so vividly that he gags. The terror that accompanies this recall is absolute, so overwhelming that he has to physically stop whatever he is doing, often stumbling away to a quiet corner of the warehouse, his heart hammering against his ribs until the present moment slowly reasserts itself. His coworkers have learned to keep their distance, seeing him as aloof or easily startled, unaware of the war he is fighting in the silent aisles of stacked pallets.

Confrontation of any kind has become unbearable. His shift supervisor is a loud, demanding man, prone to raising his voice over minor infractions. Whenever the supervisor begins to shout, whether at Binh or another worker, Binh feels that same boyhood helplessness rise in his throat. He is certain that any argument will escalate into physical violence, that he will be thrown to the ground again. To avoid this, he has become meticulously compliant, never questioning an order and taking circuitous routes through the massive building to avoid the supervisor’s office. This has made him less efficient, earning him a quiet warning about his productivity last month—a consequence that only deepens his anxiety.

Over the last several months, these experiences have become more frequent. The avoidance that once kept him safe now feels like a shrinking cage. He stopped taking the bus for fear of being jostled and pinned in a crowd. He eats his meals alone to avoid any chance of a disagreement or an unexpected touch. The final impetus for seeking help came last week, when a new, well-meaning coworker grabbed his arm to stop him from backing into a forklift. The sudden restraint triggered a flashback so intense that Binh cried out and fell to his knees, right there on the concrete floor. The shame of the incident, coupled with the terrifying realization that he was losing control in the one place he needed to feel stable, was what finally brought him to therapy. He expressed a simple, profound fear: that one day, the memory will come and he won’t be able to find his way back.
